messages.author: 5914e579c97f1326
messages.subject: Incorporating Survey Design in CAR model in R INLA
parts:
I have survey data at individual level, with PSU (primary sampling unit), Strata( subnational unit and rural/urban) and survey weights. In addition, I have levels of education for education for each participant correlated over time.

I need to specify a small area estimation model(SAE), that accounts for the survey design, has both space, time and space-time terms. The output should be subnational unit with s.e and CIs.

I have previous experience of doing SAE using aggregated data that do not have a particular survey design. The approach has been based on the following example from  Spatial and Spatio-temporal Bayesian models with R-INLA


formula.intIV<- y ~ f(ID.area,model="bym",graph=Georgia.adj) +
  f(ID.year,model="rw2") +
  f(ID.year1,model="iid") + 
  f(ID.area.int,model="besag", graph=Georgia.adj,group=ID.year.int,control.group=list(model="rw2"))

mod.intIV <- inla(formula.intIV,family="poisson",data=data,E=E, 
                  control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE), 
                  control.compute=list(dic=TRUE,cpo=TRUE))

How to adapt this formulation to individual data and incorporate the survey design?

Thanks 
Peter

What is missing from your description is precisely _how_ you want to build the sampling design into the model. In contrast to frequentistic estimators, a Bayesian model requires an explicit probabilistic construction. Thus you need to explain the hierarchical model structure, showing precisely where and how the sampling design comes in. Once we have that information, we may be able to say what that means in terms of r-inla code.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Incorporating Survey Design in CAR model in R INLA
parts:
The below is the information available for survey design: 


Enumeration areas (EA) are selected, using a two-stage sample design from a national sampling frame. In addition, the sampling frame is divided into subgroups/strata that are as homogeneous as possible using subnational unit and by rural/urban within the subnational unit.

 

In the first stage of selection, the primary sampling units (PSUs) are selected with probability proportional to size within each stratum.  The PSUs are typically census enumeration areas (EAS).  The PSU forms the survey cluster. In the second stage, a complete household listing is conducted in each of the selected clusters. Following the listing of the households a fixed number of households (about 25) is selected by equal probability systematic sampling in the selected cluster.

 

Sampling weights are adjustment factors applied to each case in tabulations to adjust for differences in probability of selection and interview between cases in a sample, due to either design or happenstance and differential response rates are also made.

 

In my data I have the PSU, the subnational unit and the survey weights 


Peter

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Incorporating Survey Design in CAR model in R INLA
parts:
Thanks for the details!

It's not clear to me that the "sampling weights" need to be used here.
If you model all the unknowns (i.e. the non-observed households that
could _potentially_ have been observed) and the sampling scheme
doesn't depend on the observed quantities, than those weights are only
needed by certain frequentistic estimators.
However, if your model is only built on the aggregated PSU level (or
the sampling scheme depends on observables, directly or indirectly),
then yes, they do need to be considered.
But you'll need to decide how to incorporate them in, as describing
the entire sampling scheme isn't really feasible in R-INLA.

I'm not a SAE expert, but I believe the analogue to the frequentistic
approximations is to use the weights as multipliers on the
log-likelihoods?
This can be done with
inla(..., weights = ...)

From ?inla :

weights: Fixed (optional) weights parameters of the likelihood, so the
log-likelihood[i] is changed into
weights[i]*log-likelihood[i]. Default value is rep(1,
n.data). Due to the danger of mis-interpreting the results
(see below), this option is DISABLED by default. You can
enable this option for the rest of your ‘R’ session, doing
‘inla.setOption(enable.inla.argument.weights=TRUE)’. WARNING:
The normalizing constant for the likelihood is NOT
recomputed, so ALL marginals (and the marginal likelihood)
must be interpreted with great care. Possibly, you may want
to set the prior for the hyperparameters to ‘"uniform"’ and
the integration strategy to ‘"eb"’ to mimic a
maximum-likelihood approach.

Finn

messages.author: d560d9e01924933c
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Incorporating Survey Design in CAR model in R INLA
parts:
Dear all,

I have some thought on using sampling weights on Bayesian models, in
particular in INLA.

The sampling weights are not the same as the weights parameter in
INLA. The weights parameter in INLA is the same as lm or glm functions
where they simply replicate that observation, in other terms in a
potential term for the likelihood,

Suppose a generic model with a parameter theta

Y|theta ~ G(y | theta)

Le y_1, y_2,...,y_N a random sample of Y, then the likelihood is defined as

L(theta) = \prod_{i = 1}^{N} g(y_i | theta )

Suppose the y_1 appears w_1 times, y_2 w_2,...,y_n w_n times and
sum_{j=1}^{n} w_j = n so the likelihood can be rewritten as

L(theta) = \prod_{i = 1}^{N} g(y_i | theta ) = \prod_{j = 1}^{n} g(y_j
| theta )^{w_j}

The w's are the weight parameter implemented in INLA. And they are
definitely not the sampling weights which usually they add up the
population size.

You could normalize the sampling weights such as they add up the
sample size and run in INLA, but you have to be in mind the you are no
longer dealing with the likelihood but with a Pseudo-Likelihood
instead, and therefore you would have the pseudo posterior. You may be
interested a paper by Savitsky and Toth (2016)
https://projecteuclid.org/euclid.ejs/1468847267

There are some other approaches to sampling data, but the pseudo
posterior approach is the by far the easiest one to implement in INLA,
and it would work on your model.

I hope it helps, it would have helped me two years ago when I was
looking for dealing with the same issue. :-)

Cheers,
Leo
